prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made it possible to measure time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B057, Katori and Ye) as my single-part position, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened the reasons. The discovery content is the magic-wavelength condition: a lattice wavelength at which the light shift cancels between the clock states. That condition turned a trapped-atom clock from a clever idea into an instrument that interrogates thousands of atoms at once, and it is a new principle, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. Ye's group then showed what that buys, by taking systematic uncertainty and stability to about 1e-18 and bringing collisions, spin-orbit coupling and correlated ensembles under control. The maturity test I apply to any instrument is reproduction with independent systematics. Here JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, SYRTE, PTB and Chinese groups do reproduce it, and frequency-ratio campaigns and fibre links compare the clocks with each other. The measured consequences already exist: centimetre- to millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifts of constants and on ultralight dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. On attribution, eight openings named exactly Katori and Ye and no other shortlisted candidate has that. The citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and the demonstrated 1e-18 performance. It should not mention the redefinition of the second, which is a standards decision and a consequence of the discovery, not a condition for it. It should also avoid presenting the clock as a spin-off of the comb, so that it stays distinct from 2005 and 2012. I am not asking the committee to decide on support counts. All eight members ranking B057 only tells me nobody doubts the science, and the case rests on that science.
statement.case_against: The most serious objection is that this is the third prize in optical metrology in twenty years (2005 comb, 2012 ion control), and a reader may take it as refinement of a recognised line. A fair reply is that the lattice clock rests on a different mechanism, but I accept that Mehlig and Danielsson are drawing a real line and I cannot show it is not a judgement call. Credit is the second risk: Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups made real contributions to particular milestones, and a two-name citation leaves them out. I consider these follow-on to the concept and the 1e-18 demonstration, but I concede that the historical record is not as single-threaded as the unanimous opening proposals suggest. Third, B015 has the stronger claim to having opened a new field of matter. That is a different virtue from the one I am rewarding, and the committee has to choose which virtue it values more this year. I do not think the choice can be settled by argument alone.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle graphene first for a simple mechanism with a decisive experiment and consequences across a new field, and ranks clocks seventh because much post-2010 progress is systematic refinement and the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: Bernhard, I agree with half of your demand: the citation must state what is new in principle, and I would write it around the magic-wavelength condition, not a record number that another group could pass. That is why my citation names the lattice. I do not agree that post-2010 progress is mere refinement. Getting from 1e-15 to 1e-18 required controlling blackbody shifts, lattice hyperpolarisability, collisions and density shifts, and the many-body understanding of the lattice clock came out of that work and was not part of the original proposal. On waiting for the redefinition, the discovery is complete and verified irrespective of the CGPM timetable. Your simple-mechanism argument for B015 is persuasive as science, but a continuum model that predicts a magic angle and a quantity that independent laboratories can measure to eighteen digits are different kinds of evidence. I would be comfortable with either of us being wrong about the ordering, but I am not convinced by the claim that a new platform outranks a quantified advance by default.

responses.point: Ranks B015 first on the original-experiment test (2018 Jarillo-Herrero result at the predicted angle), calls B057 her first alternative, and notes that the record performance came from several groups including Lemonde, Gill and NIST, building on the comb.
responses.response: Eva, your original-experiment test is the right one and I would apply it to both candidates. For clocks, the original idea (Katori's magic wavelength, with the first strontium lattice demonstration) and the decisive performance frontier (Ye) are two documented, separable contributions, and the NIST and SYRTE results you mention validated and extended them. They did not originate the principle. For B015, I want the same test: the 2018 experiments were a team effort in which Yuan Cao is first author, so the three-name limit forces a choice that your trio does not fully resolve. I accept that moire matter has opened more physics that could not be seen before, and I would not oppose B015 on the merits. My remaining concern is that its decisive physics, the pairing mechanism, is still open, whereas for clocks the physics claimed in the citation is the part that is settled. I note that you have said you would not object to a clock prize, and I take that at face value.

responses.point: Ranks B015 first as a prediction-experiment loop reproduced by many groups, places clocks eighth because it follows the 2005 and 2012 prizes and its payoff, the redefinition, is still ahead, but lists B057 as the strongest fallback and defers to Kroll and Lindroth on whether Ye is as decisive as Katori.
responses.response: Olle, thank you for the deference, and here is my answer on Ye. Katori supplied the magic-wavelength concept and the first demonstration, which is the discovery. Ye's contribution is not a refinement of it: his group's strontium lattice clock moved the whole field to the quantum-limited many-atom regime and showed 1e-18 stability and accuracy, which is what made the concept a measurement tool for geodesy and fundamental tests. I would regard a Katori-only prize as the less defensible reading of the record. On your argument that the payoff is still ahead, the payoffs I count are measured now, in redshift sensing across a centimetre and in bounds on varying constants. The unfinished redefinition is neither a payoff nor a condition. On your fallback, if the committee concludes that B015's attribution cannot be made clean (Yuan Cao, Dean, Lopes dos Santos), then B057 is where I think the room converges, and you have said you would not oppose it.

responses.point: Keeps B057 first, keeps B035 as an alternative and not a joint prize because credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and Mlynek is contested and 1997 overlaps, and prefers the fundamental-physics emphasis to geodesy and devices.
responses.response: Eva, you and Pearce were right to resist my round-1 ranking of atom interferometry second. The credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Müller and others is contested, and the 1997 cooling prize overlaps the early work, so B035 cannot be paired with B057 inside a three-person limit without a split I could not defend. I now treat B035 only as a fallback. Your point about emphasis also changes what I would write: the persuasive part is quantum-limited coherent control of many atoms and the control of systematics, and geodesy and applications are consequences that belong in the background text. I would keep the single two-name configuration for that reason.

responses.point: Prefers B053 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the theory-then-experiment chain, admits the attribution gap around Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the overlap with the 2016 prize, and says B015 or B054 would be cleaner if credit cannot be settled.
responses.response: Ulf, I agree that topological insulators are a major conceptual advance and that the experimental chain is real. I still cannot rank B053 above B057 because of the problem you state yourself: three names cannot cover Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang without leaving a visible gap, and no two members who rank it would use the same trio. By your own standard that the credit must be settled before the committee commits, B057 is the candidate where it is. I also take your caution about 2016 seriously, which is the same type of objection that has been made to clocks against 2005 and 2012. I cannot say that one overlap is clearly weightier than the other, and I would like the committee to treat both objections with equal care.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a distinct principle (magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation) or as a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control line. I hold the first view, but Mehlig and Danielsson hold a defensible alternative.

Whether Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg or Ludlow should be added to the credit. A three-name limit would allow it, but I have not found a contribution that is separable from the Katori concept and the Ye performance frontier.

Whether eight years of reproduction without a settled pairing mechanism is enough maturity for B015. My own view is that I do not have the condensed-matter expertise to settle that, and I would defer to Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson on the reproducibility of the phases and on the twist-angle disorder question.

Whether a two-part prize would be wiser given a committee split between measurement advance and field-opening novelty. I have not found a pairing that fits the three-person limit without weakening both parts.
statement.conflict_note: I have no recusal-level conflict on B057 and I disclose these connections. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is a JILA scientist of the Hall group, but I have no joint work with Ye or Katori. My recent work on laser stabilisation with slow light concerns ultrastable lasers, which are central to optical clocks. I am on the WACQT executive team, which overlaps institutionally with Goran Johansson's Chalmers home and bears on B021 only; B021 is not in my configuration, and I would abstain from deciding it. B048 and B054 are not touched by any tie of mine. I will keep these disclosures on the record for the vote.
